cases.title: External attack surface management
cases.scenario: After an acquisition, a customer finds an old support portal missing from the asset inventory. Is it still theirs?
cases.visibility: Domains, hosts and their public relationships are visible from outside. Give the product a starting organization or scope and review suggested assets.
cases.attribution: Use the domain history, subsidiary relationship and current service owner to confirm the portal belongs in the inventory.
cases.owner: Exposure management identifies the asset. Infrastructure confirms ownership and resolves the finding.

cases.title: Public API discovery
cases.scenario: The mobile app still works after the old customer portal is retired. Which API host or endpoints support it?
cases.visibility: An outside-in service can look for API hosts in an agreed scope. A traffic-based service needs requests to pass through its network. A configuration-based option needs read-only access to cloud or code systems.
cases.attribution: Match the host or observed route to a gateway, application and team. Ask which endpoints would be invisible without traffic.
cases.owner: The API platform owner and application team decide whether to keep, protect or retire it.

cases.title: DNS and certificate monitoring
cases.scenario: A campaign ends. Its old subdomain still points to a retired service, and a certificate appears for a similar hostname. Who owns each?
cases.visibility: DNS records and certificates in public transparency logs are observable. Configure the relevant domains or organization for ongoing alerts.
cases.attribution: Check the exact hostname, certificate name and service record against what the DNS and certificate owners intended.
cases.owner: DNS operations reviews stale records. The PKI team investigates unexpected issuance.

cases.title: Third-party attack surface monitoring and ratings
cases.scenario: A payroll provider’s security rating drops. Which finding warrants a conversation with the supplier?
cases.visibility: Rating services can observe external signals. A buyer needs its supplier list and service criticality to prioritize follow-up.
cases.attribution: Ask the supplier to confirm the asset and observation. Map the affected service to the contract and business process.
cases.owner: Third-party risk contacts the supplier’s security owner and tracks the response.

cases.title: Package impersonation and dependency risk
cases.scenario: A proposed dependency differs from a familiar package name by one letter. Could it enter the company’s build?
cases.visibility: Package names and metadata can be public. A dependency alert or package request ties that evidence to a particular project or download path.
cases.attribution: Match the exact package, version and request to the repository or build. Registry-wide monitoring of a company’s brand is a separate capability to verify.
cases.owner: Developer security and the build owner review the dependency or block the request.

cases.title: Public secrets monitoring
cases.scenario: An employee accidentally publishes a company API key from a personal account. Who can identify the key and revoke it?
cases.visibility: A public commit, Gist or package can be visible outside the company. Supported sources, history and access to company-specific alerts vary by product.
cases.attribution: Separate the identity of the person who posted it from ownership of the key. Check the vendor’s attribution evidence and verification for that credential type.
cases.owner: Ask who owns triage while the issuer is unknown. The account administrator can help confirm ownership, and the service team can identify what depends on the key.

cases.title: Public code and configuration leaks
cases.scenario: A personal repository contains a file resembling an internal deployment template. Is this actually company code?
cases.visibility: Public repository content can be inspected. Available sources differ, and company-specific names or recognizable code help narrow the search.
cases.attribution: Compare the material with a known internal file and ask its maintainer to confirm the match. Check separately for embedded credentials.
cases.owner: The CTI analyst and engineering owner verify the leak and coordinate removal. AppSec handles any exposed secrets.

cases.title: Public cloud storage exposure
cases.scenario: A customer export sits in cloud storage. Can anyone read it, and who can change the permission?
cases.visibility: The two examples use connected cloud accounts and permissions. Their policies and configuration provide evidence that an outside observer may lack.
cases.attribution: Confirm the bucket or container, account owner, intended audience and effective access. Access logs are separate evidence of a download.
cases.owner: Cloud security and the data owner adjust permissions and verify the resulting access.

cases.title: Exposed documents and sharing links
cases.scenario: A supplier may have posted an internal price list. Is there an external copy, or did someone create a broadly accessible link inside the company?
cases.visibility: An external leakage service can search covered repositories. A SharePoint admin can inspect sharing-link activity in the company tenant. Each sees a different part of the incident.
cases.attribution: Have the document owner confirm the file and intended recipients. Identify which organization controls the copy or link.
cases.owner: The data owner works with supplier management on an external copy or a tenant admin on an internal sharing link.

cases.title: Does this published threat affect us?
cases.scenario: A campaign report names your industry and lists file indicators. Your SOC lead wants to know by the next briefing whether anyone found evidence in your environment and what still needs investigation.
cases.visibility: Start with the report date, targeting and indicators. Check which devices, file types and dates your team can search before interpreting a result.
cases.attribution: Record the host, time and source for a match. A file sighting establishes presence. Use process, identity or other case evidence to assess execution and impact. For an empty search, record the scope and any gaps.
cases.owner: Threat intelligence chooses indicators worth checking. The SOC searches local evidence and sends any matches to incident response. The responder briefs the owner on corroborated activity, no match within the searched scope, or insufficient coverage.

cases.title: Brand impersonation and takedowns
cases.scenario: Customers report a fake sign-in page using the company’s logo. Who can get it removed and confirm it stayed down?
cases.visibility: Lookalike domains and fake public pages can be observed externally. Legitimate brand assets and authority to act support the response.
cases.attribution: Compare the page and domain against approved properties. Identify the trademark holder and who may authorize a removal request.
cases.owner: Brand protection, fraud and legal coordinate the request and record confirmation from the host or registrar.

cases.title: Stolen workforce credentials
cases.scenario: An employee address appears in a breach record. Does it belong to a current account that needs attention?
cases.visibility: Breach and underground datasets can surface exposed credentials. These sources may require a subscription. A domain match alone cannot establish account activity.
cases.attribution: Match the identity to a current or former employee, then review identity-provider evidence before choosing a response.
cases.owner: The SOC and identity operations team review account activity and decide whether to reset credentials or revoke sessions.

cases.title: Email domain authentication and DMARC
cases.scenario: An unfamiliar service sends mail as the company after a marketing launch. Is it an approved sender with broken authentication?
cases.visibility: The DNS policy is public. Sender results depend on receiving systems submitting aggregate reports and the customer routing them to a service.
cases.attribution: Match reported sending services to approved mail platforms and business owners. DMARC addresses use of the sending domain. A separately registered lookalike belongs in brand protection.
cases.owner: Email security and DNS operations consult marketing operations before changing the sending configuration or policy.
